check.title: Hormonal control of the male reproductive system

mc.prompt: Which source → hormone → target chain is correct?
mc.cue: Match a release site and its direct target.
mc.explanation: LH is released by the anterior pituitary and stimulates testosterone-producing interstitial cells.

mc.prompt: Why can an outside androgen source reduce sperm production?
mc.answer: Negative feedback can reduce FSH and LH stimulation
options: The anterior pituitary begins making sperm instead
The androgen must block the vas deferens physically
Androgens change sperm into Sertoli cells
Negative feedback can reduce FSH and LH stimulation
mc.cue: Use the normal feedback loop rather than inventing a duct blockage.
mc.explanation: Outside androgen can suppress upstream signals, reducing support for the testis’s normal sperm-production activity.

writing.prompt: Trace two branches from GnRH to their testicular targets. Explain how the branches support sperm production.
writing.model: GnRH from the hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary. FSH supports Sertoli cells in seminiferous tubules; LH stimulates interstitial cells to release testosterone. Sertoli-cell activity and testosterone support sperm production.

writing.prompt: In a functioning feedback model, explain what rising testosterone does to its upstream stimulation. Why is this negative feedback?
writing.model: Rising testosterone inhibits hypothalamic and pituitary stimulation, reducing GnRH and LH. This tends to limit further testosterone production, opposing the initial rise. Negative refers to the opposing response, not an undesirable effect.
criteria: Traces feedback back to control centres.
Explains opposition to the original change.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Low LH with functioning interstitial cells
worked.scenario: In a simplified model, LH release falls while the interstitial cells remain capable of responding.
steps: Locate LH’s source: the anterior pituitary.
Locate LH’s target: interstitial cells in the testis.
Reduce the stimulation in the model: less LH tends to mean less testosterone release.
Consider feedback: lower testosterone reduces inhibitory feedback. If the control centres can respond, they may increase stimulation. The reason LH first fell is not established by this model.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Apply the explanation
guided.instruction: Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

items.prompt: FSH release falls. Which target loses direct stimulation first?
items.hint: FSH and LH have different targets within the testis.
items.explanation: FSH supports Sertoli-cell activity; LH is the direct signal to interstitial cells.

items.prompt: Testosterone rises above its usual level in this functioning model. What feedback response is expected?
items.hint: Trace the return arrow, not just the downward pathway.
items.explanation: Higher testosterone strengthens negative feedback, reducing upstream stimulation.

new_optional_model: FSH is directly released from inhibin's inhibitory effect and would tend to rise. The stated change concerns the Sertoli-cell/inhibin feedback loop. Testosterone feedback remains usual in this model, so the observation does not itself establish a corresponding LH rise. Distinguish the two return signals instead of predicting that every pituitary hormone changes together.
